title: The Neuron & Glia
summary: Meet the cells that build the nervous system: neurons that signal and glia that support, insulate and defend them.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Neuron

levels.kid:
A neuron is a tiny messenger cell in your brain and body. You have about 86 billion of them in your brain!

A neuron looks a bit like a tree. The branches at the top are called **dendrites**. They listen for messages from other neurons. The round middle part is the **cell body**. It is the neuron's home base and keeps it alive. The long trunk is the **axon**. It carries the message far away, like a wire. At the very end are little tips called **axon terminals**. They pass the message to the next cell.

So the message goes one way: branches, then body, then trunk, then tips. Like passing a note down a line of friends!
levels.hs:
Neurons are the signaling cells of the nervous system. The human brain contains roughly 86 billion of them, and each one has the same basic parts.

- **Dendrites**: branching extensions that receive inputs from other neurons. Many are covered in tiny bumps called dendritic spines, where most excitatory synapses sit.
- **Cell body (soma)**: contains the nucleus and the machinery for making proteins. It keeps the neuron alive.
- **Axon hillock**: the cone-shaped spot where the axon leaves the soma. Just past it is the **axon initial segment**, where the decision to fire an electrical signal (the action potential) is usually made.
- **Axon**: a single long projection that carries the signal away from the soma. Some axons are shorter than a millimeter; others run about a meter, from your spinal cord to your toes.
- **Axon terminals**: the endings that release chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) onto the next cell.

Information generally flows in one direction: dendrites, then soma, then axon, then terminals. This idea, called **dynamic polarization**, was proposed by Santiago Ramón y Cajal, who also argued that neurons are separate cells rather than one continuous web.

Neurons usually do not divide after development, which is one reason brain injuries are so serious.
levels.college:
The neuron is a highly polarized cell specialized for receiving, integrating and transmitting information.

**Somatodendritic compartment.** The soma holds the nucleus and abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum; clumps of rough ER and ribosomes stain darkly with basic dyes as **Nissl substance**. Nissl bodies extend into dendrites but are absent from the axon hillock and axon, a classic histological clue. Dendrites carry the bulk of synaptic input; dendritic spines compartmentalize calcium and biochemical signaling at individual excitatory synapses and change shape with learning.

**Axon initial segment (AIS).** The AIS has a very high density of voltage-gated sodium channels anchored by ankyrin-G, making it the usual site of action potential initiation. It also acts as a diffusion barrier helping to keep axonal and somatodendritic proteins separate.

**Axon and terminals.** The axon may branch into collaterals and ends in presynaptic terminals packed with synaptic vesicles and mitochondria. Because the axon lacks most protein-synthesis machinery, it depends on **axonal transport**: anterograde transport by kinesin along microtubules (toward the terminal) and retrograde transport by dynein (toward the soma). Retrograde transport is how some toxins and viruses, such as tetanus toxin, rabies and herpes viruses, reach the cell body.

**Cytoskeleton.** Microtubules (with tau in axons and MAP2 in dendrites), neurofilaments (intermediate filaments that set axon caliber) and actin (concentrated in spines and growth cones) shape the cell.

**Clinical link.** Cutting an axon triggers **chromatolysis** in the soma (swelling, dispersal of Nissl substance, peripheral nucleus) and **Wallerian degeneration** of the distal segment.
levels.phd:
The textbook neuron is a useful fiction, and the modern picture complicates nearly every part of it.

**Polarity and its maintenance.** Polarity is established during development when one neurite becomes the axon, and is maintained by the AIS. Ankyrin-G scaffolds Nav channels (especially Nav1.6 distally and Nav1.2 proximally in many cortical neurons), Kv7 (KCNQ) channels and βIV-spectrin, while a periodic actin–spectrin lattice and selective filtering restrict protein movement. The AIS is plastic: its length and position shift with activity, tuning excitability, a form of homeostatic plasticity.

**Dendrites compute.** Dendrites are not passive cables. Voltage-gated Na+, Ca2+ and NMDA receptor conductances support dendritic spikes, and backpropagating action potentials inform synapses about output, enabling spike-timing-dependent plasticity. Layer 5 pyramidal neurons can couple apical tuft input to somatic output through calcium plateau potentials, so a single neuron can behave like a two-layer network.

**Information flow is not strictly one-way.** Dendrites can release transmitters (dendrodendritic synapses in the olfactory bulb), and retrograde messengers such as endocannabinoids travel from postsynaptic to presynaptic sites. Dynamic polarization is a strong rule with real exceptions.

**Local translation.** mRNAs are transported into dendrites and even axons and translated locally, allowing synapse-specific protein synthesis. Disrupted local translation is implicated in fragile X syndrome (loss of FMRP).

**Transport and disease.** Kinesin and dynein run on uniformly polarized axonal microtubules (plus ends distal), whereas dendritic microtubules are of mixed polarity in mammals. Hyperphosphorylated tau detaching from microtubules underlies tauopathies; defects in dynein–dynactin and kinesin motors cause specific neurodegenerative and neuropathic disorders. Neurons are also extraordinarily energy-hungry: the brain uses about 20% of resting oxygen consumption, most of it restoring ion gradients.
levels.expert:
For a clinician or surgeon, neuronal anatomy matters because each compartment fails in a recognizable way.

**Soma injury** (neuronopathy) produces non-length-dependent deficits. Dorsal root ganglion neuronopathy, for example in paraneoplastic disease or Sjögren syndrome, gives patchy, asymmetric sensory loss including the face and trunk with early loss of reflexes and proprioception, unlike a length-dependent axonopathy.

**Axon injury** (axonopathy) is usually length-dependent: the longest axons fail first, so symptoms begin in the toes and rise to the knees before the fingertips are involved, the stocking-glove pattern of diabetic polyneuropathy. Nerve conduction studies show reduced amplitudes with relatively preserved velocities, the opposite of a demyelinating picture.

**Axonal transport** is the route for several clinically important agents. Tetanus toxin travels retrogradely to inhibitory interneurons in the cord and blocks glycine and GABA release, producing rigidity and spasms. Rabies ascends to the CNS, which is why the time to symptoms depends partly on wound location. Varicella-zoster hides in sensory ganglia and returns along the dermatome as shingles.

**After transection**, the distal axon undergoes Wallerian degeneration over days, and the cell body undergoes chromatolysis. Whether the neuron survives and regrows depends on distance from the soma, the age of the patient, and the environment: peripheral axons regenerate at roughly 1 mm per day, so a surgeon repairing a nerve near the shoulder counts months before hand muscles can be reinnervated, and motor end plates may not survive the wait. That clock drives the timing of nerve repair and nerve transfer surgery.

**Pitfall:** "neuron loss" on imaging is late. Function fails at the synapse and axon long before cell bodies disappear, which is why early disease can look normal on MRI.

keyPoints: A neuron has dendrites (input), a soma (cell body), an axon (output) and axon terminals (release)
The axon initial segment, rich in voltage-gated Na+ channels, is where action potentials usually start
Nissl substance (rough ER) is in the soma and dendrites but not the axon
Axonal transport: kinesin carries cargo toward terminals (anterograde), dynein back to the soma (retrograde)
Cutting an axon causes Wallerian degeneration distally and chromatolysis in the soma

examples.tr: It is taken up at nerve terminals and carried by retrograde axonal transport to the CNS.

test.q: Which part of a neuron mainly RECEIVES input from other neurons?
test.explain: Dendrites receive most synaptic input. The axon carries output and terminals release transmitter.

test.q: Where is an action potential usually initiated?
test.explain: The axon initial segment has a very high density of voltage-gated sodium channels, giving it the lowest firing threshold.

test.q: Nissl substance is made of:
test.explain: Nissl bodies are stacks of rough ER with ribosomes; they mark protein synthesis and are absent from the axon hillock and axon.

test.q: Which motor protein carries cargo from the soma TOWARD the axon terminal?
test.explain: Kinesin drives anterograde transport toward microtubule plus ends at the terminal; dynein carries retrograde cargo back.

test.q: Tetanus toxin and rabies virus reach the CNS by:
choices: Crossing the blood–brain barrier in the choroid plexus
test.explain: Both are taken up at peripheral terminals and ride dynein-driven retrograde transport to the cell body in the CNS.

test.q: After an axon is cut, the part distal to the cut undergoes:
test.explain: The distal segment, cut off from the soma, degenerates (Wallerian degeneration). Chromatolysis is the soma's reaction.

test.q: Which scientist argued that neurons are separate cells and that signals flow in one direction?
test.explain: Cajal championed the neuron doctrine and dynamic polarization. Golgi, who invented the stain Cajal used, believed in a continuous network.

test.q: A length-dependent axonopathy typically starts:
test.explain: The longest axons fail first, so symptoms start in the feet (stocking-glove pattern).

test.q: What is the cone-shaped region where the axon leaves the cell body called? (two words)
test.explain: The axon hillock leads into the axon initial segment, the trigger zone.

test.q: The single long process that carries signals away from the soma is the ___.
test.explain: The axon conducts the action potential to the terminals.

test.q: Microtubule-associated protein ___ is found mainly in axons and forms tangles in Alzheimer's disease.
test.explain: Tau stabilizes axonal microtubules; hyperphosphorylated tau forms neurofibrillary tangles. MAP2 is the dendritic counterpart.

test.q: The cell body of a neuron is also called the ___ (one word).
test.explain: Soma (or perikaryon) contains the nucleus and protein-synthesis machinery.

kidTest.explain: The cell body keeps the neuron alive.

kidTest.q: The message travels from branches, to body, to trunk, to the ___.
kidTest.explain: The tips (axon terminals) pass the message to the next cell.

advancedTest.q: Ankyrin-G at the axon initial segment is important because it:
choices: Clusters voltage-gated Na+ and KCNQ channels and helps maintain axon–dendrite polarity
advancedTest.explain: Ankyrin-G is the master scaffold of the AIS; losing it causes axons to acquire dendritic features.

advancedTest.q: Which finding most strongly suggests a sensory NEURONOPATHY rather than a length-dependent axonopathy?
choices: Asymmetric sensory loss including the face and trunk with early global areflexia
advancedTest.explain: Dorsal root ganglion cell-body loss is not length-dependent, so deficits are patchy, can involve the face/trunk, and reflexes are lost early.

advancedTest.q: In mammalian dendrites, microtubule polarity is:
advancedTest.explain: Axons have uniform plus-end-out microtubules; mammalian dendrites have mixed polarity, which helps sort cargo.

advancedTest.q: Loss of which RNA-binding protein, which regulates local dendritic translation, causes fragile X syndrome? (abbreviation)
advancedTest.explain: FMRP (encoded by FMR1) represses translation of many synaptic mRNAs; its loss causes fragile X.

lessons.title: Types of Neurons

levels.kid:
Not all neurons look the same. They come in different shapes for different jobs.

**Sensory neurons** are like reporters. They tell your brain what you feel, like a hot stove or a soft blanket.

**Motor neurons** are like bosses giving orders. They tell your muscles to move, like kicking a ball.

**Interneurons** are like the middle people on a phone call. They connect neurons to each other inside your brain and spinal cord. Most of your neurons are interneurons!

Shapes are different too. Some neurons have one branch, some have two, and some have lots of branches like a big bushy tree. Each shape is just right for its job.
levels.hs:
Neurons can be sorted in two main ways: by what they do and by their shape.

**By function:**
- **Sensory (afferent) neurons** carry information from receptors toward the central nervous system (CNS). Example: neurons that detect touch on your fingertip.
- **Motor (efferent) neurons** carry commands away from the CNS to muscles and glands.
- **Interneurons** connect neurons within the CNS. They are by far the most common type and do most of the "thinking."

A memory trick: **A**fferent **A**rrives, **E**fferent **E**xits.

**By shape (number of processes leaving the soma):**
- **Multipolar**: one axon and many dendrites. Most neurons, including motor neurons and pyramidal cells of the cortex.
- **Bipolar**: one dendrite and one axon on opposite sides. Found in special senses such as the retina, the olfactory epithelium and the inner ear.
- **Pseudounipolar**: a single process that splits into two branches, one going to the skin or muscle and one to the spinal cord. These are the sensory neurons whose cell bodies sit in the dorsal root ganglia.
- **Unipolar**: one process; common in invertebrates.

Some neurons are named after their looks or discoverer, like **Purkinje cells** in the cerebellum, with huge fan-shaped dendrites.
levels.college:
Neuronal classification combines morphology, connectivity, neurotransmitter and, increasingly, gene expression.

**Morphological classes.**
- **Multipolar** neurons dominate the CNS. Pyramidal cells (cortex, hippocampus) have a triangular soma, an apical dendrite and basal dendrites, and are glutamatergic projection neurons. Alpha motor neurons in the ventral horn are large multipolar cells. Purkinje cells, the sole output of the cerebellar cortex, are GABAergic with a planar dendritic arbor.
- **Bipolar** neurons serve special senses: retinal bipolar cells, olfactory receptor neurons, and spiral and vestibular ganglion neurons.
- **Pseudounipolar** neurons (dorsal root ganglia and most cranial sensory ganglia) have one stem process that bifurcates into a peripheral and a central branch. Functionally the peripheral branch behaves like an axon: it conducts action potentials and is often myelinated.

**Projection vs local circuit neurons.** Golgi type I neurons have long axons leaving the region (pyramidal cells, motor neurons); Golgi type II neurons have short axons that stay local (most interneurons).

**Excitatory vs inhibitory.** In the cortex roughly 80% of neurons are excitatory glutamatergic cells and about 20% are inhibitory GABAergic interneurons. Interneuron subtypes are often defined by markers: parvalbumin (fast-spiking basket and chandelier cells targeting soma and AIS), somatostatin (Martinotti cells targeting distal dendrites) and VIP (often inhibiting other interneurons, causing disinhibition).

**Other functional classes.** Upper motor neurons (cortex, brainstem) project to lower motor neurons (ventral horn, cranial motor nuclei). Autonomic neurons form a two-neuron chain: preganglionic in the CNS and postganglionic in a ganglion. Neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus release hormones into the blood.
levels.phd:
Classical schemes are being replaced by multimodal cell-type taxonomies, and the question "how many neuron types are there?" has become an empirical one.

**Transcriptomic taxonomy.** Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing, combined with Patch-seq (electrophysiology, morphology and transcriptome from the same cell), has identified on the order of thousands of transcriptomic clusters across the mouse brain and over a hundred in a single cortical area. These clusters are organized hierarchically: class (glutamatergic, GABAergic, non-neuronal), subclass (for example L5 extratelencephalic vs intratelencephalic projection neurons; Pvalb, Sst, Vip, Lamp5 interneurons), and finer types. Many types grade into one another along continua rather than forming discrete islands, raising the conceptual problem of whether "type" is a natural kind.

**Developmental origin.** Cortical excitatory neurons derive from dorsal pallial progenitors and migrate radially, whereas cortical GABAergic interneurons are born in the ganglionic eminences of the ventral telencephalon (Pvalb and Sst types mainly from the medial ganglionic eminence, Vip and Lamp5 types largely from the caudal ganglionic eminence) and migrate tangentially. Origin predicts much of adult identity.

**Projection classes matter clinically and computationally.** Extratelencephalic (pyramidal tract) neurons of layer 5 send axons to brainstem and cord; these include the giant Betz cells of primary motor cortex, which degenerate in ALS. Intratelencephalic neurons stay within cortex and striatum.

**Species differences.** Human cortex shows expanded supragranular layers and specialized cell types, such as rosehip interneurons described in human layer 1, and human pyramidal dendrites have distinct cable properties. Rodent findings therefore do not always transfer.

**Disease selectivity.** Selective vulnerability is a type-level phenomenon: dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta in Parkinson's disease, medium spiny neurons of the striatum in Huntington's disease, and Pvalb interneuron dysfunction in some epilepsies and schizophrenia models.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, neuron type determines the pattern of disease, and pattern recognition is how neurologists localize.

**Motor neuron classes.** Upper motor neuron (UMN) loss gives spasticity, hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response; lower motor neuron (LMN) loss gives weakness, atrophy, fasciculations and hyporeflexia. ALS is the classic disorder of both: a patient with a wasted, fasciculating hand and brisk reflexes in the same limb has a combination no single lesion of a nerve or root explains. Spinal muscular atrophy is pure LMN (anterior horn cell); primary lateral sclerosis is pure UMN.

**Sensory neuron classes.** Large-fiber neurons (proprioception, vibration) and small-fiber neurons (pain, temperature, autonomic) fail separately. Large-fiber loss gives sensory ataxia and a positive Romberg sign; small-fiber neuropathy gives burning feet with a normal nerve conduction study, because routine conduction studies only measure large myelinated fibers. Skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fiber density is the test that captures it.

**Selective vulnerability in practice.** Purkinje cells are among the most vulnerable to hypoxia, alcohol and some paraneoplastic antibodies (anti-Yo), giving a pancerebellar syndrome. Hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons are especially susceptible to global ischemia, which is why cardiac arrest survivors can have profound amnesia with otherwise preserved function. Interneuron dysfunction is the target in many genetic epilepsies; in Dravet syndrome, loss of Nav1.1 mostly impairs inhibitory interneurons, which is why sodium channel blockers can worsen seizures in that condition.

**For the surgeon.** Mapping in awake craniotomy is functional cell-type mapping in effect: stimulating primary motor cortex activates corticospinal (Betz and other layer 5) output, and motor evoked potentials during spine surgery monitor that same pathway. Protecting these projection neurons and their axons is the core of safe resection near eloquent cortex.

keyPoints: By function: sensory (afferent), motor (efferent) and interneurons; interneurons are the most numerous
By shape: multipolar (most neurons), bipolar (special senses), pseudounipolar (dorsal root ganglia)
Pyramidal cells are excitatory projection neurons; Purkinje cells are the inhibitory output of the cerebellar cortex
Upper motor neurons project to lower motor neurons in the brainstem and ventral horn
Different neuron types are selectively vulnerable in different diseases

examples.tr: Combined UMN and LMN signs, the hallmark of ALS.

lessons.title: Glial Cells

levels.kid:
Neurons get all the attention, but they have helpers called **glia**. "Glia" comes from a word meaning glue!

- **Astrocytes** are star-shaped helpers. They feed neurons and clean up around them, like a kitchen crew.
- **Oligodendrocytes** wrap neurons' wires in a fatty coat called myelin, like tape around a cable, so messages go fast.
- **Microglia** are the guards. They eat germs and clean up broken bits.
- **Ependymal cells** line the hollow spaces in your brain and help make the brain's special water.

Without glia, neurons could not do their jobs. They are the team behind the star players!
levels.hs:
Glial cells (glia) are the non-neuronal cells of the nervous system. For a long time they were thought to be just "glue," but they do essential work. In the human brain, glia and neurons are roughly equal in number.

**CNS glia:**
- **Astrocytes**: star-shaped cells that support neurons. They wrap blood vessels with their "end-feet" and help form the **blood–brain barrier**, recycle neurotransmitters such as glutamate, balance potassium levels, store glycogen and form scars after injury.
- **Oligodendrocytes**: make myelin in the brain and spinal cord. One oligodendrocyte can myelinate segments of many different axons.
- **Microglia**: the brain's immune cells. They patrol, engulf debris and germs, and prune unneeded synapses during development. Unlike other glia, they come from the immune system (yolk sac), not from neural tissue.
- **Ependymal cells**: line the ventricles and central canal. Specialized ependymal cells in the choroid plexus help produce cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

**PNS glia:**
- **Schwann cells**: myelinate peripheral nerves, one segment of one axon per cell.
- **Satellite cells**: surround neuron cell bodies in ganglia.

Most brain tumors that start in the brain itself come from glia, which is why they are called **gliomas**.
levels.college:
Glia are a heterogeneous group with distinct lineages, molecular markers and functions.

**Astrocytes** (marker: GFAP; also ALDH1L1, AQP4) are of two classic types: protoplasmic (gray matter) and fibrous (white matter). Their perivascular end-feet express aquaporin-4 and the inward-rectifier K+ channel Kir4.1, supporting water and K+ homeostasis (spatial buffering). Astrocytes take up glutamate through EAAT1/EAAT2 transporters and convert it to glutamine via glutamine synthetase; glutamine returns to neurons for transmitter resynthesis (the glutamate–glutamine cycle). They induce tight-junction properties in endothelium, the true structural barrier of the BBB. After injury they become reactive and form a **glial scar**.

**Oligodendrocytes** (Olig2, MBP, PLP) derive from oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs, NG2+), which persist in the adult brain and can remyelinate. One oligodendrocyte myelinates internodes on up to dozens of axons, so losing one cell demyelinates many axons.

**Microglia** (Iba1, CX3CR1, TMEM119) derive from yolk-sac macrophage progenitors that colonize the brain early in development. They survey the parenchyma continuously and prune synapses using complement tags (C1q, C3).

**Ependymal cells** are ciliated cuboidal cells lining the ventricles; choroid plexus epithelium, a specialized ependyma with tight junctions, forms the blood–CSF barrier. **Tanycytes** line the third ventricle floor and link CSF to the hypothalamus.

**PNS glia:** Schwann cells (S100, myelin protein P0) myelinate one internode of a single axon, or ensheathe many small unmyelinated axons in Remak bundles. Satellite glia surround ganglion cell bodies.

**Clinical correlates:** gliomas (astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, ependymoma), multiple sclerosis (oligodendrocyte/myelin injury), neuromyelitis optica (antibodies against AQP4 on astrocytes) and Guillain–Barré syndrome (Schwann cell/myelin or axonal injury).
levels.phd:
Glia are active participants in circuit function, and the field has moved from "support cell" to partner.

**The tripartite synapse.** Astrocyte processes ensheathe many synapses, regulate extracellular glutamate and K+, and display intracellular Ca2+ signals in response to transmitters. Whether astrocytes release "gliotransmitters" (glutamate, D-serine, ATP/adenosine) at physiological rates remains debated, partly because classic manipulations (for example IP3R2 knockout) had confusing results. D-serine as an NMDA receptor co-agonist, and adenosine-mediated sleep pressure, are among the better-supported roles.

**Metabolic coupling.** The astrocyte–neuron lactate shuttle hypothesis proposes that astrocytes take up glucose, glycolyse it and supply lactate to neurons; the quantitative importance in vivo is contested, but oligodendrocytes similarly supply metabolites to axons via monocarboxylate transporter MCT1, and loss of this support causes axonal degeneration independent of myelin.

**Adaptive myelination.** OPCs receive synapses from axons and respond to activity; new myelin forms during motor learning, and blocking oligodendrogenesis impairs learning a new motor skill in mice. Myelin is therefore a plastic regulator of conduction timing, not a fixed insulator.

**Microglia and synapses.** Microglial pruning of complement-tagged synapses refines developing circuits (for example in the retinogeniculate system). Aberrant complement-mediated pruning has been implicated in schizophrenia (C4A copy-number variation) and early Alzheimer's disease. TREM2 variants that impair microglial responses raise Alzheimer's risk, placing microglia in the causal chain rather than only reacting to pathology.

**Reactive astrocyte states.** Reactive astrocytes are heterogeneous; some states support repair, while others (induced by microglial IL-1α, TNF and C1q in mouse models) lose supportive functions and become neurotoxic. Binary "A1/A2" labels are now considered too simple.

**Glymphatic hypothesis.** Perivascular CSF flow, dependent on astrocytic AQP4, may clear solutes such as amyloid-β, particularly during sleep; the mechanism and magnitude are actively disputed.
levels.expert:
For a clinician, glia are the substrate of some of the most common and the most lethal neurological diseases.

**Glial tumors.** Diffuse gliomas are classified by molecular markers, not only histology. IDH-mutant astrocytomas, IDH-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas and IDH-wildtype glioblastoma behave very differently; glioblastoma is the most common malignant primary brain tumor in adults. Diffuse gliomas infiltrate along white matter tracts, so even a "gross total" resection leaves tumor cells beyond the visible margin. That biology is why surgery is combined with radiation and chemotherapy, and why maximal safe resection, guided by mapping and fluorescence agents such as 5-aminolevulinic acid, is the surgical goal rather than a cure.

**Astrocytopathy.** Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder is driven by antibodies to aquaporin-4 on astrocyte end-feet. It causes severe optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (three or more vertebral segments) and area postrema syndrome (intractable hiccups, nausea, vomiting). Distinguishing it from MS matters because some MS drugs can worsen NMOSD.

**Oligodendrocyte and myelin injury.** MS plaques are areas of oligodendrocyte loss and demyelination; remyelination by OPCs is incomplete with age. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is JC virus infection of oligodendrocytes in immunosuppressed patients, a feared complication of some immunotherapies. Osmotic demyelination syndrome follows overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia and damages the central pons.

**Microglia and the scar.** After stroke or trauma, reactive astrocytes form a scar that walls off damage but also blocks axon regrowth, one reason spinal cord injuries do not heal like peripheral nerves.

**Edema.** Cytotoxic edema in early ischemia involves astrocyte swelling, visible as restricted diffusion on MRI; vasogenic edema around tumors reflects BBB breakdown and responds to corticosteroids, whereas cytotoxic edema does not.

keyPoints: CNS glia: astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia and ependymal cells; PNS glia: Schwann cells and satellite cells
Astrocytes support the blood–brain barrier, clear glutamate and K+, and form scars
Oligodendrocytes myelinate many CNS axons; each Schwann cell myelinates one segment of one PNS axon
Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells and come from yolk-sac progenitors, not neural tissue
Gliomas, MS, NMOSD and PML are diseases of glia

test.explain: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons; Schwann cells do it in the PNS.

test.q: Which glial cell is the brain's resident immune cell?
test.explain: Microglia patrol, phagocytose debris and pathogens, and prune synapses.

test.q: Microglia originate from:
test.explain: Unlike other CNS glia, microglia are of mesodermal (myeloid) origin.

test.q: Astrocyte end-feet surrounding capillaries help maintain the:
test.explain: Astrocytes induce and support the endothelial tight junctions of the BBB.

test.q: Which cells line the ventricles?
test.explain: Ependymal cells line ventricles and the central canal.

test.q: A key difference between oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells is that:
choices: One oligodendrocyte myelinates segments of many axons; one Schwann cell myelinates one segment of one axon
test.explain: That one-to-many vs one-to-one relationship is a classic exam point.

test.q: Astrocytes convert glutamate into:
test.explain: Via glutamine synthetase; glutamine goes back to neurons (glutamate–glutamine cycle).

test.q: Antibodies against aquaporin-4 cause:
test.explain: AQP4 is on astrocyte end-feet; NMOSD is an astrocytopathy.

test.q: Which marker is classically used to identify astrocytes?
test.explain: Glial fibrillary acidic protein is the classic astrocyte marker; Iba1 marks microglia.

test.q: Satellite cells are found:
choices: Around neuron cell bodies in peripheral ganglia
In the cerebral cortex as myelin makers
test.explain: Satellite glia surround somata in sensory and autonomic ganglia.

test.q: Tumors that arise from glial cells are called ___ (one word).
test.explain: Astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, ependymomas and glioblastoma are gliomas.

test.q: The scar formed by reactive astrocytes after CNS injury is called the glial ___.
test.explain: The glial scar limits damage but also blocks axon regeneration.

test.q: The PNS glial cell that myelinates peripheral axons is the ___ cell.
test.explain: Named after Theodor Schwann.

kidTest.q: What are glia?
kidTest.explain: Glia are the helpers.

kidTest.q: Which helper is star-shaped and feeds neurons?
kidTest.explain: Astro means star!

kidTest.q: Which helper is the guard that eats germs?
kidTest.explain: Microglia are the guards.

kidTest.q: Oligodendrocytes wrap neurons in a fatty coat called ___.
kidTest.explain: Myelin is like tape around a wire.

kidTest.q: The word glia comes from a word meaning...
kidTest.explain: Glue! People once thought glia just held neurons together.

kidTest.q: Do glia help messages go faster?
kidTest.explain: Myelin from glia speeds up messages.

advancedTest.q: A patient has severe bilateral optic neuritis and a spinal cord lesion spanning 5 vertebral segments, plus a week of intractable hiccups. Best next test?
advancedTest.explain: Longitudinally extensive myelitis + optic neuritis + area postrema syndrome = NMOSD; check AQP4-IgG (and MOG-IgG).

advancedTest.q: Which is the most accurate statement about oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) in adults?
choices: They persist, receive synapses from axons and can generate new myelinating oligodendrocytes
advancedTest.explain: Adult OPCs (NG2 glia) are abundant and support remyelination and adaptive myelination.

advancedTest.q: TREM2 variants raise Alzheimer's risk mainly by impairing the function of:
advancedTest.explain: TREM2 is a microglial receptor needed for responses to amyloid and debris.

advancedTest.q: Peritumoral vasogenic edema responds to corticosteroids, but early ischemic cytotoxic edema does not. Why?
choices: Vasogenic edema reflects BBB leakage that steroids reduce; cytotoxic edema is intracellular swelling from energy failure
advancedTest.explain: Steroids tighten the leaky tumor vasculature; they do not fix failed Na+/K+ pumps in ischemia.

lessons.title: Myelin, Schwann Cells & Nerve Repair

levels.kid:
Many neurons have long wires called axons. Lots of these wires wear a fatty coat called **myelin**. Myelin is like the plastic around a phone charger cable. It keeps the message from leaking and makes it go super fast.

The coat has little gaps. The message jumps from gap to gap, like a kid hopping across stepping stones in a river. That is much faster than walking slowly through the water!

If a wire in your arm or leg gets hurt, it can slowly grow back, because special helpers called **Schwann cells** make a tunnel to guide it. In the brain and spinal cord, wires have a much harder time growing back. That is why doctors work so hard to protect them.
levels.hs:
**Myelin** is a fatty, insulating layer wrapped around many axons. It is made by glial cells that wind their membranes around the axon many times: oligodendrocytes in the CNS and Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system (PNS). Myelin is about 70–80% lipid, which is why myelinated tracts look white ("white matter").

Myelin is not continuous. It comes in segments called **internodes**, separated by small bare gaps called **nodes of Ranvier**. Voltage-gated sodium channels are packed at the nodes, so the electrical signal "jumps" from node to node. This **saltatory conduction** is much faster and more energy-efficient than conduction along an unmyelinated axon. Thick myelinated axons can conduct at over 100 meters per second, while thin unmyelinated pain fibers conduct at around 1 meter per second.

**Nerve injury and repair.** When a peripheral nerve is cut, the part beyond the cut degenerates (Wallerian degeneration). Schwann cells then clear debris, line up into guiding tubes and release growth factors, so the axon can regrow about 1 mm per day. In the CNS, regrowth mostly fails: oligodendrocyte myelin contains growth-blocking molecules, and astrocytes form a scar.

Diseases that strip myelin include **multiple sclerosis** (CNS) and **Guillain–Barré syndrome** (PNS).
levels.college:
**Structure.** Compact myelin consists of tightly apposed membrane wraps. Key proteins differ by compartment: CNS myelin is rich in proteolipid protein (PLP) and myelin basic protein (MBP), plus myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) on the outer surface; PNS myelin relies on myelin protein zero (P0), PMP22 and MBP. Each node of Ranvier is flanked by **paranodes**, where myelin loops attach to the axon via a contactin/Caspr/neurofascin-155 junction, and **juxtaparanodes**, which cluster voltage-gated K+ (Kv1) channels beneath the myelin. Nodes concentrate Nav channels anchored by ankyrin-G and neurofascin-186.

**Function.** Myelin increases membrane resistance and decreases membrane capacitance, so current spreads farther and less charge is needed to depolarize the next node. Conduction velocity in myelinated fibers rises roughly linearly with diameter, compared with roughly the square root of diameter in unmyelinated fibers.

**Peripheral nerve anatomy.** Each axon with its Schwann cell lies in endoneurium; axons group into fascicles wrapped by perineurium (which forms the blood–nerve barrier); the whole nerve is wrapped in epineurium.

**Injury classification.**
- **Neurapraxia** (Seddon) / Sunderland I: focal conduction block, often demyelinating, axon intact; recovers in weeks.
- **Axonotmesis** / Sunderland II–IV: axon disrupted with variable damage to connective tissue; Wallerian degeneration occurs; recovery depends on regeneration.
- **Neurotmesis** / Sunderland V: complete transection; needs surgical repair.

**Regeneration.** Denervated Schwann cells convert to a repair phenotype (c-Jun-dependent), form bands of Büngner and secrete neurotrophins. Regeneration proceeds at roughly 1 mm/day. In the CNS, inhibitors such as Nogo-A, MAG and OMgp (acting via NgR1 and others), chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans in the scar and low intrinsic growth capacity of adult neurons limit regrowth.
levels.phd:
Myelin biology sits at the intersection of biophysics, cell biology and evolution.

**Biophysics.** Cable theory explains why myelination pays off: with internodal capacitance cut and resistance raised, the length constant increases and nodal Nav current recharges the next node quickly. The optimal ratio of axon diameter to total fiber diameter (the g-ratio) is about 0.6–0.7 in peripheral nerve on theoretical and empirical grounds, although CNS axons often deviate. Recent modeling and imaging suggest the periaxonal space and internodal leak are not negligible, so the "perfect insulator" picture is an approximation.

**Myelination is regulated.** In the PNS, axonal neuregulin-1 type III signalling through ErbB2/3 on Schwann cells sets whether and how thickly an axon is myelinated; axons above about 1 µm diameter are generally myelinated. In the CNS, oligodendrocyte myelination is less dependent on neuregulin, is partly activity-dependent, and continues into the third decade in human association cortex, paralleling cognitive maturation.

**Node assembly differs by system.** PNS nodes form when Schwann cell microvilli (gliomedin) cluster neurofascin-186 and Nav channels; CNS nodes depend more on paranodal junctions and extracellular matrix. Autoantibodies against nodal and paranodal proteins (neurofascin-155, contactin-1, Caspr1) define the "nodopathies," a subset of chronic inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy with distinct treatment responses.

**Genetics.** PMP22 dosage is a striking example of gene-dose sensitivity: duplication causes Charcot–Marie–Tooth type 1A, deletion causes hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies. PLP1 duplication causes Pelizaeus–Merzbacher disease. GJB1 (connexin-32) mutations cause X-linked CMT.

**Regeneration research.** Intrinsic growth programs (mTOR pathway, PTEN deletion, KLF family, SOX11) can drive CNS axon regrowth in rodents. In the PNS, the bottleneck is often distance and time: chronically denervated Schwann cells lose their repair phenotype and muscle end plates degenerate, so accelerating regeneration (for example brief electrical stimulation after repair) matters more than starting it.
levels.expert:
For a neurosurgeon, myelin biology turns into decisions about when to wait and when to operate.

**Classifying a nerve injury.** A sharp laceration with complete deficit suggests neurotmesis: explore and repair early, ideally within days, with a tension-free epineurial or group-fascicular repair; a gap is bridged with a nerve graft (commonly sural nerve) or a conduit for short gaps. A closed stretch or contusion injury is usually observed: clinical exam and EMG at around 3 months look for reinnervation. No recovery by about 3–6 months prompts exploration with intraoperative nerve action potentials; a recordable action potential across the lesion favors neurolysis over resection and grafting.

**The clock.** Motor end plates deteriorate after prolonged denervation, typically in the range of 12–18 months, after which reinnervation may fail even if axons arrive. Because axons grow about 1 mm/day, a proximal brachial plexus injury may never restore hand function by direct repair. That is the rationale for **nerve transfers**: moving a nearby expendable motor branch close to the target muscle, for example ulnar fascicle to the biceps branch (Oberlin transfer) to restore elbow flexion.

**Electrodiagnosis.** Demyelination shows slowed conduction velocity, prolonged distal latency, conduction block and temporal dispersion; axon loss shows reduced amplitudes and, after 2–3 weeks, fibrillation potentials on EMG. Testing too early, before Wallerian degeneration, can mislead.

**Demyelinating disease.** Guillain–Barré syndrome (acute, monophasic, ascending weakness with areflexia, albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF) can progress to respiratory failure; monitoring vital capacity matters. Treatment is IVIG or plasma exchange. CIDP evolves over more than eight weeks and often responds to steroids, unlike classic GBS. In the CNS, MS lesions are periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal.

**Pitfall:** a "Saturday night palsy" (radial nerve compression) is usually neurapraxia and recovers in weeks; operating on it is a mistake.

keyPoints: Myelin is lipid-rich insulation made by oligodendrocytes (CNS) and Schwann cells (PNS)
Nodes of Ranvier concentrate Na+ channels, enabling fast saltatory conduction
Seddon classification: neurapraxia, axonotmesis, neurotmesis
Peripheral axons regenerate roughly 1 mm per day, guided by Schwann cells (bands of Büngner)
CNS regeneration is limited by myelin inhibitors (Nogo-A, MAG, OMgp) and the glial scar

test.q: The gaps between myelin segments are called:
test.explain: Nodes of Ranvier are the bare gaps rich in Na+ channels; internodes are the myelinated segments.

test.q: Saltatory conduction means:
choices: The signal jumps from node to node
The signal travels only in dendrites
test.explain: Saltare = to jump; depolarization regenerates only at nodes.

test.q: Myelin speeds conduction mainly by:
choices: Decreasing capacitance and increasing membrane resistance
Adding more Na+ channels along internodes
test.explain: Less charge needed per segment and less leak means current spreads farther and faster.

test.q: Which Seddon injury is a conduction block with an intact axon?
test.explain: Neurapraxia: axon intact, usually focal demyelination; recovers in weeks.

test.q: A completely transected nerve (neurotmesis) usually needs:
test.explain: With the nerve cut through, the ends must be repaired (or grafted).

test.q: Peripheral axons regenerate at roughly:
test.explain: About 1 mm/day (about an inch a month).

test.q: Which molecule is a myelin-associated inhibitor of CNS axon regeneration?
test.explain: Nogo-A (with MAG and OMgp) inhibits regrowth in the CNS. P0 is a PNS compaction protein.

test.q: Multiple sclerosis damages myelin in the:
test.explain: MS is a CNS demyelinating disease; GBS is the PNS counterpart.

test.q: The connective tissue layer surrounding a single fascicle is the:
test.explain: Perineurium wraps fascicles and forms the blood–nerve barrier.

test.q: Thin unmyelinated pain (C) fibers conduct at about:
test.explain: Around 0.5–2 m/s, versus more than 100 m/s for large myelinated fibers.

test.q: What Schwann-cell columns guide regenerating peripheral axons? (bands of ___)
test.explain: Bands of Büngner are aligned repair Schwann cells inside the old endoneurial tubes.

test.q: Myelinated tracts look white because myelin is mostly ___.
test.explain: Myelin is about 70–80% lipid.

test.q: CNS myelin is made by ___.
test.explain: PNS myelin is made by Schwann cells.

kidTest.q: What is myelin like?
choices: The plastic coat on a cable
kidTest.explain: It insulates the wire, like plastic on a charger cable.

kidTest.q: Myelin makes messages go...
kidTest.explain: Faster!

kidTest.q: The message jumps gap to gap like...
kidTest.explain: Like hopping across stepping stones.

kidTest.q: Nerves in your arm can grow back with help from ___ cells.
kidTest.explain: Schwann cells make a guiding tunnel.

kidTest.q: Is it easier for wires to grow back in your arm or in your brain?
kidTest.explain: Arm (peripheral) nerves regrow much better.

advancedTest.q: Duplication of PMP22 causes CMT1A. Deletion of the same gene causes:
choices: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies
advancedTest.explain: HNPP results from PMP22 deletion; PLP1 duplication causes Pelizaeus–Merzbacher; GJB1 causes X-linked CMT.

advancedTest.q: A closed brachial plexus stretch injury shows no clinical or EMG recovery at 4 months. The most appropriate step is:
choices: Surgical exploration with intraoperative nerve action potential recording
advancedTest.explain: Exploration at about 3–6 months; a recordable NAP across the lesion favors neurolysis, absence favors resection and grafting or transfer.

advancedTest.q: Why are nerve transfers used for proximal injuries instead of relying only on direct repair?
choices: Regeneration at about 1 mm/day may not reach distal muscles before motor end plates degenerate
advancedTest.explain: Moving a donor nerve close to the target shortens the distance and beats the denervation clock.

advancedTest.q: Fibrillation potentials on EMG after axonal injury typically appear after about how many weeks? (number range like 2-3)
advancedTest.explain: Spontaneous fibrillations need Wallerian degeneration and denervation to develop, roughly 2–3 weeks.
